WORRY GUIDE — LIFE

When you're torn over saying no

You open the reply screen and close it — it's been half a day. Your feeling that you want to say no is clear, yet you can't find the courage to send it. If you decline, will the relationship suffer? Will you be thought of as cold? Whether you accept or decline, dragging it around even after you have decided is what makes this decision so wearing. To be clear at the outset, saying no is not an act that breaks a relationship. Continuing to accept beyond your limits is what makes a relationship heavy later. This page guides you through how to draw the line.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

When you can't say no and feel torn, what is wavering is not only your assessment of the request itself. One factor is not wanting to disappoint the other person. It is kindness at its root, but if you keep putting the other person's reaction ahead of your own limits, there will be a backlash somewhere. The second is your self-image of wanting to be a good person. It is not declining itself, but resistance to being someone who declines, that drags the indecision out. The third is that the problem is not the content of the request but the volume. Each one may be small, but stacked together they steadily press on your time. While the reasons stay mixed, you feel as if there is no reason to say no, and you keep accepting. Starting by separating the three is the entrance to sorting this out.

POINT 02

How to sort it out

When you're torn, first write out the conditions under which you could accept. Until when would it be all right? How far could you go without it becoming a burden? Once the conditions are visible, the options widen from the two-way choice of accept or decline to a third shape: accepting with changed conditions. Move the deadline, narrow the scope, take on only part of it. If the conditions still don't fit, then declining is the answer. This writing goes more easily if you do it while drawing a card and looking at it. The card does not produce a conclusion; it is a mirror reflecting your current state — whether you are tired, or moving out of a sense of obligation. If you keep a record in a log of what you declined and what you accepted, it helps the next time the same person asks. Once you can see your own pattern of drawing lines, the time you spend torn gets shorter.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

In situations where you're torn over saying no, cards that speak to drawing lines, limits, holding off, and adjustment can offer useful clues.

Justice, shown holding scales and a sword, represents fair line-drawing. Whether it is fair to the other person and to you becomes the standard for saying no.

The Ten of Wands is a figure carrying more wands than they can hold. It is a sign of taking on too much, showing that you are close to your limit.

The Two of Swords shows someone frozen, balancing two swords. It is the state itself of being unable to decide and continuing to hold off.

Temperance is an angel pouring water between two cups. It offers a perspective for adjusting the conditions and finding just the right middle ground for accepting.

The Fool shows someone stepping out lightly with a single bundle. It reminds you of the option of answering lightly, without thinking too heavily about it.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. Is the reason you want to say no the content, the volume, or the timing? If one condition changed, could you accept? If you declined, what are you afraid of — the other person's reaction, or your own self-image? What happened afterward with requests you forced yourself to accept in the past? How much room do you have left right now to take on? Once your answers are together, all that is left is to communicate. Briefly, without lining up too many reasons, and with an alternative if you have one. That is how to say no without breaking the relationship.

FAQ

Frequently asked questions

Won't saying no make my relationship with the other person worse?

More than declining clearly, accepting vaguely and pulling out at the last minute is what damages a relationship. If you decline early, briefly, and with an alternative, the other person can make their next move too. The stress of carrying something you couldn't decline is more harmful to a long-term relationship.

What is happening at the point where I'm torn over saying no?

In many cases, you are not torn over the request itself, but imagining the other person's reaction when you decline. The content of the request you have already judged; anxiety about being evaluated is what stops the decision. Separate out what the anxiety really is, and the answer comes closer.

How should I draw the line when I do accept?

Rather than all or nothing, decide the range you can manage — this much I can do — first, and present it. Set a boundary on even one of deadline, volume, or number of times, and it becomes a shape without strain for both the other person and you. Showing a range is not declining; it is negotiating conditions.

Say no, or accept with changed conditions? Why not sort out, through the questions the cards raise, both your feelings for the other person and your own limits?
